subject: pharmacology
title: Long-Acting Muscle Relaxants, Sugammadex Reversal, and Spasmolytics

steps.tx: The historic long-acting bisquaternary aminosteroid non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent is **pancuronium**. Providing complete skeletal muscle paralysis spanning ninety to one hundred twenty minutes, pancuronium is excreted predominantly by the kidneys. It uniquely exhibits vagolytic activity by blocking cardiac M2 muscarinic receptors and inducing sympathetic norepinephrine release, producing characteristic sinus tachycardia and hypertension that benefits cardiothoracic surgery while complicating ischemic heart disease.
steps.say: Pancuronium provides long-acting muscle paralysis but causes vagolytic sinus tachycardia and hypertension.

steps.tx: Instantaneous pharmacological reversal of rocuronium-induced and vecuronium-induced neuromuscular blockade is achieved using **sugammadex**. A chemically modified gamma-cyclodextrin with eight lipophilic cavity side chains, sugammadex encapsulates free steroidal neuromuscular blockers in plasma at a 1:1 molecular stoichiometry. This tight chelation lowers free drug concentration to zero, driving rapid dissociation of rocuronium from motor endplate receptors and restoring full voluntary muscle power within three minutes.
steps.say: Sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium in a 1:1 molecular ring, reversing profound paralysis within three minutes.

steps.tx: The life-saving definitive antidote for malignant hyperthermia crises triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine is **dantrolene**. Functioning as a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant, dantrolene binds specifically to the ryanodine receptor type 1 (RyR1) on sarcoplasmic reticulum membranes. By blocking uncontrolled calcium release into the myoplasm, dantrolene terminates hypermetabolic muscle rigidity, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and lethal body temperature spikes.
steps.say: Dantrolene blocks sarcoplasmic ryanodine receptors to halt uncontrolled calcium release in malignant hyperthermia.

steps.tx: Centrally acting antispasticity therapy for managing muscle rigidity in multiple sclerosis and spinal cord transection relies on **baclofen**. As a lipophilic derivative of gamma-aminobutyric acid, baclofen selectively stimulates metabotropic GABAB receptors coupled to Gi proteins in the spinal dorsal horn. Receptor activation increases potassium conductance and inhibits voltage-gated calcium channels, hyperpolarizing motor interneurons and suppressing mono- and polysynaptic spastic stretch reflexes.
steps.say: Baclofen activates spinal GABAB receptors to suppress hyperactive reflexes in spasticity.

steps.tx: Reducing spasticity without inducing severe voluntary skeletal muscle weakness is achieved with the centrally acting agent **tizanidine**. Tizanidine functions as a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist in the brainstem and spinal cord. By stimulating presynaptic alpha-2 receptors on spinal interneurons, it inhibits release of excitatory amino acids like aspartate and glutamate, diminishing painful flexor spasms with substantially less direct muscle flaccidity than baclofen.
steps.say: Tizanidine activates central alpha-2 receptors to suppress spastic reflexes while preserving voluntary muscle strength.

steps.tx: The historic natural plant alkaloid extracted from Chondrodendron tomentosum arrow poisons is **tubocurarine**. Functioning as the classical prototype non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, tubocurarine competitively antagonizes nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate. However, its tendency to induce profound histamine release and block autonomic sympathetic ganglia causes bronchospasm and severe hypotension, leading to its complete replacement by modern synthetic relaxants.
steps.say: Tubocurarine is the historical prototype competitive blocker that fell out of favor due to histamine release and hypotension.

steps.tx: Non-depolarizing muscle relaxants achieve flaccid surgical paralysis through competitive antagonism at the **skeletal motor endplate**. Competitive blockers bind to one or both alpha subunits of the pentameric nicotinic acetylcholine receptor without triggering channel opening. By physically obstructing acetylcholine access, they prevent endplate depolarization; when seventy-five to eighty percent of receptors are occupied, transmission fails and voluntary muscular contraction ceases completely.
steps.say: Competitive blockers occupy motor endplate nicotinic receptors, preventing acetylcholine from opening cation channels.

steps.tx: Objective clinical quantification of intraoperative neuromuscular blockade depth requires electric peripheral nerve stimulation and the **train-of-four ratio**. Four supramaximal electrical impulses delivered at two hertz to the ulnar nerve evoke adductor pollicis twitches. Non-depolarizing relaxants cause progressive twitch fade; clinical recovery sufficient for safe tracheal extubation requires a train-of-four ratio of the fourth twitch height to first twitch exceeding 0.9.
steps.say: Safe tracheal extubation requires a train-of-four ratio over 0.9 to prevent postoperative respiratory failure.

vis.caption: Train-of-four monitoring assesses motor endplate nicotinic receptor recovery to guide safe reversal and extubation.
